case_study_insert.main_stem: Thornfield Dairy Produce (TDP) is a cooperative in the dairy-processing sector, employing a workforce of 65. Founded in 1998 by Marta Thornfield, it supplies cheese and yoghurt to regional supermarket chains and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TDP plans to invest $960,000 in a new cheese-making and cold-storage facility on its existing site, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year for its retail customers. TDP faces two operational problems: milk-spoilage waste of 4.1% and absenteeism of 8% among production staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The dairy packed 24,000 units last quarter at a spoilage rate of 4.1%, down from 5.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 a month. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 750 shoppers found that 61% would pay up to $0.35 more for farm-assured cheese and 55% check animal-welfare labels. Training records show 18 of 65 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new pasteuriser; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thornfield Dairy Produce as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.2% from $13.20 to $14.02 an hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills. (3) Feed and milk input costs have risen 11.5% year-on-year, food-price inflation is 7.3% and consumer spending on farm-assured cheese grew 4.0% in the same period.

questions.question_text: TDP plans to fund part of its cold-storage expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TDP of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $360,000 needs no interest payments or capital repayments, so TDP avoids adding debt-service costs to fixed costs of $360,000 a year while it already carries a $600,000 bank loan. The cash saved can be spent on reducing the 4.1% milk-spoilage waste or on training the 18 of 65 staff still needing induction on the pasteuriser, protecting the $6.00 contribution earned on each of 90,000 units.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps decision-making inside the cooperative and avoids conditions a lender might attach to a $600,000 facility, such as limits on further borrowing or security over the new cold store. Because TDP has autocratic leadership in a hierarchical structure, using internally generated funds lets Marta Thornfield and the committee control the $960,000 project without external interference, and no extra interest exposure arises if the 8% absenteeism rate temporarily reduces output. Retaining profit also avoids the risk that a lender calls in the loan if sales dip.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TDP's $360,000 retained profit, loan, waste and staffing.

questions.question_text: TDP is launching a new farm-assured cheese range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TDP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A TV advert could reach millions and quickly build awareness of the farm-assured label across the country. For a 65-member cooperative with $360,000 fixed costs, however, production and airtime charges are high and much of the audience buys no cheese or lies outside the regional supermarket catchment, so a large share of the spend is wasted. It would also compete with repayments on the $600,000 loan funding the $960,000 cold store.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is affordable, reaches the core shoppers near TDP's supermarkets and works well for a time-limited launch message. Its clear limitation is reach: TDP needs to sell 90,000 units a year, and local listeners alone cannot generate that volume; radio also cannot show the farm-assured and animal-welfare story visually.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can explain animal-welfare credentials to the 61% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.35 more and the 55% who check welfare labels, at low cost per person reached and with measurable engagement. Results build gradually and depend on influencer credibility, but the targeting matches the research precisely.

Recommendation: TDP should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the identified segment nationally, costs far less than television and supports the premium needed for a $6.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as too expensive and untargeted; radio is rejected because its reach is too narrow for TDP's regional supermarket growth plans.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited TDP context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in TDP's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: TDP's milk-spoilage waste is 4.1% and absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for TDP of using team working to address these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets the 65 employees share responsibility for spoilage, so workers can check each other's handling of milk and immediately spot practices that cause the 4.1% waste rate. Because staff closest to the pasteuriser understand the causes, group problem-solving can protect the $6.00 contribution on each of 90,000 units more effectively than hierarchical instructions alone, reducing waste without spending more on the $960,000 facility.

Point 2: Working in teams gives members social support and a sense of belonging, which can improve morale and reduce the 8% absenteeism rate. Lower absence means fewer disruptions to the 24,000 units packed each quarter and less need to retrain staff; with 18 of 65 workers still to complete on-the-job training at $950 a head for college courses, stability lowers training costs and helps maintain the cooperative's delivery schedule to regional supermarkets.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of team working (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to TDP's 4.1% spoilage, 8% absence and training needs.

questions.question_text: TDP must upskill 18 staff to operate the new pasteuriser. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should TDP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Instruction at the pasteuriser is specific to TDP's own equipment and hygiene standards, involves no fees and keeps the 18 trainees productive while learning, protecting the 24,000 units packed last quarter and progress made in cutting spoilage from 5.6% to 4.1%. Its weaknesses are that experienced operators must train alongside their normal duties, mistakes during learning could add to the 4.1% spoilage, and there is no external certificate that supermarkets might value.

Off-the-job training: The college course at $950 per employee totals $17,100 for 18 staff, a small sum next to the $960,000 investment, and provides structured teaching plus a recognised qualification. The trade-off is that 18 of 65 workers are away from the line, reducing short-term capacity and possibly worsening 8% absenteeism pressure, and the course may not match TDP's exact pasteuriser settings without follow-up coaching.

Decision: TDP should choose on-the-job training first and add short college modules later for senior operators. It is machine-specific, avoids $17,100 in fees and keeps output steady while waste is still 4.1%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 18 of 65 staff would disrupt cheese deliveries and risk the spoilage target, and the generic course cannot replace plant-specific instruction.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited TDP context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in TDP's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TDP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four applied uses: margin of safety of 30,000 units; average total cost of $12.00; labour productivity of about 1,385 units per worker; servicing the $600,000 loan.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $360,000 ÷ $6.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TDP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing 60,000 break-even units with output of 90,000 units shows a margin of safety of 30,000 units, so the cooperative has a substantial buffer against the 4.1% spoilage rate.
2. Average total cost of $360,000 ÷ 90,000 + $8.00 = $12.00 a unit benchmarks the cost of each cheese unit and highlights waste.
3. Labour productivity of 90,000 units ÷ 65 staff = about 1,385 units a worker helps judge whether the 8% absence rate is affordable.
4. Contribution of $6.00 sets the volume needed to service the $600,000 bank loan used for the $960,000 cold store.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TDP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TDP's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.38 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.58 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.88 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $42,000 cash = $317,000; 2025 current assets = $150,000 + $120,000 + $70,000 = $340,000. Dividing by $230,000 and $215,000 current liabilities gives 1.38 and 1.58. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($317,000 − $180,000) ÷ $230,000 = 0.60; 2025 = ($340,000 − $150,000) ÷ $215,000 = 0.88.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The current ratio rose from 1.38 to 1.58 as current assets increased by $23,000 and current liabilities fell by $15,000, giving a stronger cushion for paying suppliers. The acid test rose from 0.60 to 0.88, and this is the stronger evidence of genuine improvement because it removes $180,000 of stock in 2024 and $150,000 in 2025; with milk-spoilage waste at 4.1%, some inventories may be slow to sell. Cash rose from $42,000 to $70,000, which helps the cooperative meet bills while servicing a $600,000 loan. The concern is that trade receivables climbed from $95,000 to $120,000, so cash is tied up with supermarkets, and the acid test below 1 means TDP still cannot cover all current liabilities without stock.

Conclusion: TDP's liquidity has improved, since both ratios are higher and the gain does not come from holding more inventory. However, the acid test of 0.88 shows the improvement is incomplete, so the cooperative should chase outstanding receivables before borrowing further for the $960,000 facility.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little accurate ratio calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years, evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities, and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TDP of offering farm-assured cheese.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: In a survey of 750 shoppers, 61% said they would pay up to $0.35 more for farm-assured cheese and 55% check animal-welfare labels. That supports a higher price than $14.00 and protects the $6.00 contribution per unit against 11.5% feed and milk inflation. The badge also differentiates TDP's cheese on regional supermarket shelves and could help sell the 90,000 units needed to justify the $960,000 cold-storage investment.

Disadvantage: Meeting farm-assured standards can raise the $8.00 variable cost per unit through higher feed or welfare costs, and the insert does not decompose that cost, so the exact increase cannot be stated. If the $0.35 premium is not accepted across the range, margin falls. There is also a risk that any welfare failure damages the 55% of label-checking shoppers and worsens the current 4.1% spoilage and quality reputation just as TDP expands, while the $600,000 loan still needs servicing.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using TDP's survey data, costs and spoilage.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in feed and milk input costs will affect TDP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): On a variable-rate $600,000 ten-year loan the extra charge is 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). This is small compared with $360,000 fixed costs, and zero if the rate is fixed. The rise may make consumers more cautious and dearer future borrowing, but TDP can limit the effect by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.02 an hour): With a workforce of 65 this affects many pay packets and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours or individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The defensible check is labour productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 65 staff = roughly 1,385 units each, so the increase is sustainable only if that productivity is maintained or output rises, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (11.5% feed and milk): The $8.00 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole $8.00 rose 11.5%, that is $0.92 a unit (0.115 × $8.00), or $82,800 a year across 90,000 units. Even a partial pass-through would sharply cut contribution, though the $0.35 farm-assured premium and 4.0% demand growth can offset some of it.

Conclusion: The 11.5% rise in feed and milk costs will have the greatest impact because it hits every unit produced and directly threatens the $6.00 contribution backing the $960,000 investment. The interest effect is a known $4,500 and the wage effect depends on unstated hours, whereas input inflation is large, continuous and harder to pass on quickly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited TDP application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on TDP's costs and finance in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes and concludes feed and milk inflation has the greatest impact with reasons.
